description:
Hey! I'm putting together a team for the NASA Space Apps Challenge this weekend (Nov 14-15) and I'm looking for 3-4 coders to build with.

I'll take care of the design, documentation, and pitch. It's fully virtual, so you can be anywhere in the world.

looking for:
• Intermediate level or above in Python, JavaScript, or similar
• Some experience with APIs or working with data
summary: Moon Mirror is a transparent, reproducible method that ranks five Earth sites by how closely they match the Moon’s south pole, where Artemis bases are planned. We compared Iceland (Askja), Haughton Crater, the Antarctic Dry Valleys, Death Valley and the Atacama on five specific measured traits: coldest temperature, rainfall, surface material, latitude and ground ice. Each trait is scored by its distance from the Moon’s value, and the scores are combined into one number from 0 to 1. The Dry Valleys came out closest (0.64), followed by Haughton Crater (0.59). The winner stays the same when any one trait counts double. This addresses the challenge by giving mission planners a clear, sourced way to choose where to test equipment and train crews on Earth for safety and accuracy. It matters because no Earth site matches the Moon on every condition, so planners need to see which sites match on which traits, and use that data to their advantage affectively.
details:
What it does and how it works: We chose the Moon’s south pole as the target and found its value for each trait, mostly from NASA’s LRO Diviner temperature data and NASA’s Artemis candidate landing region information. We found the same five values for each Earth site, with a source link for every number. A Python script scores each site as a proximity value of 0 (being completely different) to 1 (being completely similar) then combines the five scores with weights (equal by default). It also runs a sensitivity check, making each trait count double in turn.

Benefits and intended impact: Anyone can see exactly where each number came from, change the weights, and add a new site by adding one row of data since everything is open sourced. The intended impact is to help planners pick analog sites for the traits that matter most for a given test, enhance accuracy and minimise fatal errors.

Tools and software: Python (pandas, matplotlib) in Google Colab, Google Sheets for data collection, HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the interactive website, GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting. We used Claude to build the website.

How it is creative: The website has live sliders, so visitors set their own weights and watch the ranking change, and cards for each site update with it. We also added a sensitivity check so the result isn’t tied to one weighting.

Factors we considered: consistent units (Kelvin, mm per year), scoring against the full range of each trait, how much weights change the result, and data limits. We state those limits openly: five sites only, mixed temperature types, a Haughton rainfall stand-in from Resolute, Nunavut, an approximate Death Valley latitude, and surface and ground-ice scores that are judgement calls.
dataRefs: NASA Identifies Candidate Regions for Landing Next Americans on Moon
